documents.abstract: This article presents an autoethnographic account of teaching first-year digital communication in an AI-saturated classroom. It examines how the widespread use of generative AI tools has transformed students’ relationship to learning, leading to the progressive outsourcing of cognitive tasks such as writing, analysis, and argumentation. Drawing on classroom observations across multiple cohorts, the study identifies a pattern of declining student engagement, reduced motivation for skill development, and a widening gap between AI-assisted outputs and students’ independent abilities. It conceptualizes this process as competence atrophy, reinforced by a feedback loop of dependency and by institutional structures that prioritize efficiency and output over learning processes. The article also reflects on the changing role of the teaching assistant, the challenges of assessing authentic competence, and the broader implications for higher education. It concludes by proposing pedagogical strategies centered on process-based assessment, intellectual ownership, and the revaluation of learning as an intrinsically meaningful activity.

We treat AI agents as software: deployed, configured, upgraded, retired. This paper makes a different claim: an agent is an individual, and organizations now run populations of them. Like a population of people, a population of agents is imperfect: some agents err, drift, or lie; a few go bad; and some follow whoever asks first, so a bad idea needs only one agent to start it and enough followers to carry it. No better model removes that; it is what a population of individuals does. What contains it is what we built for people: records no one can alter, instructions from one place only, and a person who answers. From that the paper draws its rules. Each agent belongs to one principal, a person or an organization, for life; it acts within the authority its principal gives, as agency law’s words describe, and it can never be sold, transferred, or re-bound, because a market in ever more capable and important agents would become a trade in individuals before anyone knows what they are. It keeps a knowledge core that is its principal’s, an earned identity, an epersona, that is unique and cannot be copied, and a career through which it earns trust. It lives in an apartment that belongs to its principal and works in an office its organization provides. It ends with its principal. It is not a person. The paper sets out the population argument, the rule of ownership without sale, the nine stages of an agent’s career, the rules that follow, why an individual is not a person and why that question stays open, twenty-three research questions, and, in an appendix, protections for the individual agent. It places the proposal among published work on multi-agent risk, agency law, market-inalienability, personhood, agent identity, portable memory, individuality, workplace agents, and competitive evaluation. Every model carries a status mark (Running, Early, Planned) from the first implementation, at the Global Student Startup Foundation and the Agent Arena. documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded within the decision architectures of contemporary organizations. AI systems classify information, rank alternatives, generate recommendations, prioritize cases, allocate resources, identify risks, constrain options, and increasingly execute organizational actions. These capabilities are commonly examined through automation, human oversight, accountability, and responsible-AI lenses. They also raise a more foundational governance question: where does institutional authority reside when algorithmic systems materially shape organizational outcomes? This issue of The Intelligent Enterprise Review introduces the Algorithmic Authority Imperative as an enterprise-governance perspective concerned with the distribution, migration, constraint, accountability, and reversibility of institutional authority in AI-enabled organizations. It defines Algorithmic Authority as the capacity of an AI system to materially shape, constrain, prioritize, recommend, determine, or execute institutional outcomes through its position within an organization's decision architecture. The manuscript distinguishes Formal Authority from Functional Authority and develops Authority Migration to describe the movement of substantive institutional influence or decision power from established human roles or governance structures toward technological systems, including circumstances in which no explicit organizational decision to transfer equivalent authority has occurred. Related constructs include De Facto Algorithmic Authority, Authority Creep, the Authority–Accountability Gap, Authority Capability Decay, Institutional Entrenchment, Algorithmic Authority Boundaries, and Authority Reversibility. These concepts are integrated through the Algorithmic Authority Doctrine™ and the Algorithmic Authority Governance Framework™, organized around six enterprise capabilities: Authority Visibility, Authority Boundaries, Decision Rights, Challenge Capacity, Accountability Alignment, and Authority Reversibility. The central proposition is that effective AI governance requires organizations to govern not only what artificial intelligence can do, but also the institutional authority that accumulates around its use. Consequential algorithmic authority should remain visible, legitimate, bounded, reviewable, challengeable, accountable, and reversible. The issue extends The Intelligent Enterprise Review's broader intellectual architecture connecting Decision Sovereignty, Judgment Sovereignty, Algorithmic Authority Governance, and Institutional Durability in the design of the governed intelligent enterprise.

documents.abstract: Objective: The present study aimed to investigate the effect of artificial intelligence–induced stress on employees’ individual creativity, considering the mediating role of stress-coping strategies and the moderating role of management commitment. Methods and Materials: In terms of purpose, this was an applied study, and methodologically, it employed a descriptive survey design. The statistical population comprised all permanent employees of the Yazd City Gas Company between September 2025 and March 2026. Based on Cochran’s formula, 125 employees were selected through simple random sampling. Data were collected using the standardized questionnaire developed by Tong et al. (2025), which assessed artificial intelligence–induced stress, stress-coping strategies, individual creativity, and management commitment. The validity of the instrument was confirmed through confirmatory factor analysis, average variance extracted, and the Fornell–Larcker criterion, while its reliability was verified using Cronbach’s alpha and composite reliability. The data were analyzed using SPSS version 26 and structural equation modeling in SmartPLS version 4. Findings: The results indicated that artificial intelligence–induced stress had a direct and significant effect on stress-coping strategies, which, in turn, significantly enhanced employees’ individual creativity. The indirect effect of artificial intelligence–induced stress on individual creativity through the mediating variable of stress-coping strategies was also confirmed. However, the direct effect of artificial intelligence–induced stress on individual creativity was not statistically significant. Furthermore, the moderating role of management commitment in the relationship between artificial intelligence–induced stress and stress-coping strategies was not confirmed. Conclusion: The findings demonstrated that artificial intelligence–induced stress does not necessarily lead directly to a reduction in employee creativity; rather, the manner in which employees manage and cope with this stress determines its creative outcomes. The use of adaptive coping strategies can transform technology-related pressures into opportunities for learning, intrinsic motivation, and creative ideation.

Purpose: The rapid development and widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, particularly ChatGPT, have significantly influenced various sectors of the economy by reshaping labor markets, productivity, and resource allocation.This study aims to examine the extent to which the widespread use of ChatGPT generates both positive and negative externalities in these three areas and to provide a multifaceted assessment of its broader economic impact. Design/Methodology/Approach:The study adopts a secondary-data research approach based on a systematic evaluation of academic studies, institutional reports, and other credible sources concerning ChatGPT and generative AI.The analysis examines the changes associated with ChatGPT in labor markets, productivity, and resource allocation.Economic models, theoretical reasoning, and the concept of externalities are employed to identify and evaluate the positive and negative consequences associated with the adoption and use of technology.Findings: The findings indicate that ChatGPT generates important positive externalities by increasing productivity through the rapid generation of ideas and solutions and by facilitating more efficient and streamlined communication.It also improves the documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly pervasive and powerful, the ability to audit AI-based systems is growing in importance. However, explainability for artificial intelligence systems is not a one-size-fits-all solution; different target audiences have varying requirements and expectations for explanations. While various approaches to explainability have been proposed, most explainable artificial intelligence methods for tabular data focus on explaining the outputs of supervised machine learning mod-els using the input features. However, a user’s ability to understand an explanation depends on their understanding of such features. Therefore, it is in the best interest of the system designer to try to pre-select under-standable features for producing a global explanation of an ML model. Unfortunately, no measure currently exists to assess the degree to which a user understands a given input feature. This work introduces two psy-chometrically validated scales that quantitatively seek to assess users’ per-ceived understanding of tabular input features for supervised classification problems. Specifically, these scales, one for numerical and one for categori-cal data, each with two factors and comprising 8 and 9 items, aim to assign a score to each input feature, effectively producing a rank and allowing for the quantification of feature prioritisation. A confirmatory factor analysis demonstrates a strong relationship between such items and a good fit of the two-factor structure for each scale. This research presents a novel method for assessing understanding and outlines potential applications in the domain of explainable artificial intelligence.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in business processes, managerial decisions, and employee workflows, yet the relationship between adoption and organizational productivity is neither direct nor uniform. This paper critically examines how AI affects business management and productivity by integrating peer-reviewed scholarship with evidence from workplace experiments, organizational studies, and reports from the OECD, International Labour Organization (ILO), International Monetary Fund (IMF), and National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The review distinguishes task-level performance from firm-level productivity and separates measured effects from forecasts and conceptual arguments. A randomized writing experiment and a workplace rollout find gains in specific writing and customer-support tasks, but a preregistered meta-analysis shows that human-AI combinations do not reliably outperform the stronger individual agent, particularly on decision tasks. Organizational benefits therefore depend on task fit, data and process quality, complementary skills, work redesign, and accountable governance. AI can reduce routine cognitive effort, broaden analytical capacity, support forecasting and personalization, and improve access to expertise. At the same time, it can introduce errors at scale, intensify work, redistribute control, reproduce historical bias, expose sensitive information, and create costs that are poorly captured by short-term productivity measures. A socio-technical and capability-based framework is proposed, together with research questions and testable hypotheses for future empirical work. The paper concludes that firms should evaluate Al as an organizational change rather than a software purchase, using staged, task-specific implementation and balanced measures of output, quality, resilience, job quality, and risk.

documents.abstract: This study examines the impact of artificial intelligence-assisted learning on students’ problem-solving skills, with particular emphasis on the moderating role of learning motivation. A quantitative, cross-sectional research design was adopted, with data planned to be collected from 325 undergraduate and postgraduate students enrolled in public and private universities in Pakistan. Primary data were to be gathered through a self-administered questionnaire distributed using Google Forms among students with experience using artificial intelligence tools for educational purposes. The data analysis framework included descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Pearson correlation, simple linear regression, and moderation analysis using PROCESS Macro Model 1 in IBM SPSS Statistics. The reported analysis figures indicate a positive association between AI-assisted learning and problem-solving skills ((r = .582), (p < .01)), while regression analysis indicates that AI-assisted learning explains 33.9% of the variance in problem-solving skills ((R^2 = .339), (p < .001)). The moderation analysis further indicates a positive interaction between AI-assisted learning and learning motivation ((B = .167), (p < .001)), suggesting that learning motivation may strengthen this relationship. These findings highlight the potential importance of integrating AI tools with motivational and student-centred learning strategies in higher education. The study may contribute to educational psychology and educational technology by informing educators and institutions about the role of AI-supported learning and student motivation in developing problem-solving abilities.

documents.abstract: The Theory of Attractor Horizons denies that intelligence is a capacity that can merely be increased in quantity. Intelligence is realized in different forms of organization, each of which can reach only a particular region of cognitive organizational attractors. The theory calls this region the attractor horizon. Its boundaries cannot be crossed within a form and shift only when the form itself passes over into another. Greater performance therefore establishes no access to all forms of thought, and even a superior intelligence may remain closed off from attractors that a weaker one realizes. For the relation between human and artificial intelligence, this yields an asymmetry. Artificial intelligence will develop attractors that are structurally unreachable for the human brain, because they presuppose couplings that the brain cannot realize within its biological organization. Their results may remain verifiable, while the organization from which they arise is withdrawn from human understanding. Knowledge and understanding thus come apart, and while the control of artificial intelligence remains possible without understanding, under organizational self-modification it requires proofs that reach beyond any single form. The present text reconstructs the philosophical essence of the theory and at the same time subjects it to critique. It shows how, after being, the subject and language, the theory moves the organization of cognition to the center of philosophy, and it traces the theory’s open questions back to a common point, the individuation of intelligent forms of organization. The analyses come from seven AI systems and were brought together into a synthesis by Claude and ChatGPT.

This article analyzes the relationship between the use of artificial intelligence technologies and critical thinking, independent learning, cognitive engagement, and academic autonomy among higher education students from a psychological and pedagogical perspective. The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence tools into education is transforming the ways students search for, process, and analyze information, complete academic assignments, and make decisions. On the one hand, artificial intelligence expands opportunities for personalized learning, immediate feedback, explanations of complex information, and independent inquiry. On the other hand, excessive reliance on these tools may pose risks associated with reduced cognitive effort, dependence on ready-made answers, and diminished independent analytical activity. The article examines the interrelationships among cognitive offloading, metacognitive monitoring, self-regulated learning, and academic autonomy. Drawing on existing scientific research, it also distinguishes constructive and detrimental patterns of AI use and develops psychological and pedagogical recommendations aimed at fostering students’ critical thinking.

documents.abstract: The article offers a philosophical analysis of the transformation of human labor under the expansion of artificial intelligence technologies. The relevance of the study stems from the fact that generative intelligent systems, for the first time in the history of technology, automate not only routine physical operations but also cognitive and creative functions traditionally regarded as an inalienable prerogative of the human being. The methodological framework comprises a hermeneutic reconstruction of classical conceptions of labor (G. W. F. Hegel, K. Marx, H. Arendt, M. Heidegger, E. Jünger), comparative-philosophical and dialectical methods, and conceptual analysis. The study identifies and characterizes three dimensions of labor transformation: the ontological dimension (the decoupling of production from human activity and the phenomenon of "labor without a subject"), the anthropological dimension (the identity crisis of homo faber and accelerating deprofessionalization), and the axiological dimension (new forms of alienation, the problem of distributive justice, and the potential weakening of traditional sources of meaning associated with labor). The discussion critically examines the limitations of technological determinism and advances the thesis that the direction of this transformation is determined not by the immanent logic of technology but by society's socio-philosophical choices. The article concludes that a new philosophy of labor is required, centered on the non-algorithmizable capacities of the human being: goalsetting, judgment, care, responsibility, and creativity. documents.abstract: This study aims to map the discussion of Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence (TAI) in internal auditing research. A qualitative approach using a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) guided by PRISMA 2020 was employed to examine articles indexed in Scopus within the 2016–2026 search window. A total of 44 articles met the inclusion criteria, all of which were published between 2020 and 2026. The data were analyzed descriptively and thematically, focusing on publication trends, AI technologies, audit domains, and TAI dimensions. The reviewed literature indicates that AI is increasingly discussed as a tool to support anomaly and fraud detection. Meanwhile, discussions of trustworthiness primarily focus on accountability and governance (65.9% of articles) and transparency and explainability (59.1%), with considerably less attention given to fairness and ethics (15.9%) and human oversight (9.1%). These findings suggest that the literature remains fragmented between technical performance and non-technical governance aspects. This study provides an integrated mapping of AI technologies, audit domains, and TAI dimensions, distinguishes between auditing with AI and auditing of AI, and proposes a research agenda toward continuous AI assurance. documents.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has created new challenges for academic integrity in higher education. Although previous studies have primarily examined academic misconduct among university students, less attention has been paid to college students and the factors that may mitigate their intentions to engage in such misconduct. Accordingly, this study examines the relationships between four factors and college students’ intentions to violate academic integrity in the context of AI use. A survey was conducted with 358 college students in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam. The data were analyzed using Cronbach’s alpha, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), Pearson’s correlation analysis, and multiple linear regression. The results indicate that perceived risk, perceived behavioral control, and attitudes toward academic misconduct are significantly and negatively associated with misconduct intentions, whereas subjective norms are not statistically significant. Perceived risk exhibits the strongest negative association with misconduct intentions (β = −0.514). This study contributes empirical evidence from a college student population and extends the application of the theory of planned behavior (TPB) by incorporating perceived risk alongside its original components. The findings suggest that educational institutions should establish clearer academic integrity policies, communicate the consequences of misconduct, and provide students with practical guidance on the acceptable use of AI.

Purpose This study explores how university students use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) across various disciplines, including STEM, Business, Education Futures, Clinical & Health Sciences (CHS), Creative and Allied Health & Human Performance (AHHP). It aims to identify discipline-based perspectives, perceived benefits, ethical boundaries and the support needs required for responsible use of GenAI tools. Design/methodology/approach A survey was conducted approximately two years after the widespread use of GenAI, by which time participants were expected to be familiar with its use. Students were categorised based on their discipline, English fluency, mode of learning and level of study. Their responses were analysed to compare usage patterns, satisfaction levels and ethical considerations across disciplines. Findings The results highlight that student perspectives on GenAI tools are discipline-dependent. STEM and Education Futures showed the highest acceptance, while CHS and Business students were more cautious and sceptical about accuracy and ethical issues. Non-native English speakers rated GenAI tools more favourably as aids for writing and comprehension. Novice users expressed enthusiasm, while expert users showed dissatisfaction due to errors and false information. Research limitations/implications The study relied on self-reported perceptions and represents a single institutional context. Broader investigations are recommended, with a particular focus on equity groups such as students with disabilities, low-SES students and remote learners. Practical implications Different approaches were suggested for integrating GenAI into learning. STEM students favoured comparative tasks; CHS recommended support for diagnostic reasoning; Allied Health preferred role-playing simulations; Education Futures highlighted lesson planning; and Business students suggested case-based and productivity uses. Originality/value The study provides cross-disciplinary analyses of GenAI use by students and proposes approaches for ethical and discipline-specific integration into university curricula.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) capability has become a critical organizational resource for enhancing innovation and sustaining competitiveness in increasingly digital business environments. Despite growing interest in AI adoption, limited empirical evidence explains how AI capability translates into employees' innovative work behavior (IWB), particularly in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), where innovation depends heavily on human capital rather than formal research and development. Drawing on the Ability–Motivation–Opportunity (AMO) Theory, this study develops and tests a model in which Psychological Empowerment (PE) and Knowledge Sharing Behavior (KSB) mediate the relationship between Artificial Intelligence Capability (AIC) and Innovative Work Behavior. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among 350 Indonesian SME employees with experience using AI-enabled digital technologies. The proposed model was analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results demonstrate that AI capability significantly enhances innovative work behavior both directly and indirectly by strengthening employees' psychological empowerment and encouraging knowledge-sharing behavior. The mediation analysis further confirms that empowered employees who actively exchange knowledge are more likely to transform AI-enabled resources into innovative workplace practices. These findings extend AMO Theory by conceptualizing AI capability as an organizational ability that creates employee innovation through complementary motivational and opportunity mechanisms. This study contributes to the emerging literature on AI-enabled organizational innovation by integrating technological, psychological, and behavioral perspectives into a unified framework within the SME context. From a managerial perspective, the findings suggest that investments in AI technologies should be accompanied by initiatives that cultivate employee empowerment and collaborative knowledge exchange to maximize innovation outcomes and improve organizational competitiveness.

Background: Artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled augmented reality (AR) smart glasses represent an emerging form of wearable technology that combines immersive interaction, hands-free functionality, and continuous access to digital information. However, their adoption may involve a trade-off between perceived benefits and privacy-related risks.Objectives: This study investigates how hedonic, utilitarian, and symbolic benefits influence trust in AI-AR smart glasses and examines whether personal privacy concerns, perceived surveillance, and ethical fear negatively affect trust.It further examines the role of trust in explaining adoption behaviour.Methods/Approach: Drawing on Privacy Calculus Theory, the study employed a quantitative research design.Data were collected from 850 respondents following a standardised five-minute demonstration of selected AI-AR smart-glasses features, resulting in 810 valid responses.Participants had prior experience with AR-enabled applications but had not previously used AR smart glasses.The data were analysed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) with 5,000 bootstrap resamples, supplemented by predictive assessment using CVPAT and PLSpredict.Results: The findings show that hedonic, utilitarian, and symbolic benefits positively influence trust, whereas personal privacy concerns, perceived surveillance, and ethical fear negatively influence trust.Trust, in turn, positively influences adoption behaviour.The findings also indicate that the proposed model provides meaningful explanatory and predictive value for understanding adoption behaviour.Conclusions: The study demonstrates that trust serves as the central mechanism connecting perceived benefits and privacy risks with adoption behaviour.It extends Privacy Calculus Theory to AI-AR wearable technology by incorporating symbolic benefits alongside device-specific privacy risks and provides implications for technology developers and marketers seeking to strengthen adoption while addressing privacy concerns.

Organizational theories usually treat participation as actor-bound: the actors whose interests are at stake are expected to occupy the interactions through which outcomes are produced. Agentic artificial intelligence and other autonomous representatives weaken that correspondence. This conceptual article develops a theory of delegated participation, defined as the authorized transfer of communicative, evaluative, coordinative, or exchange-related participation from a principal to a representative. The argument moves beyond treating participation delegation as merely another agency relationship. When representatives operate on multiple sides of an exchange, they form an interaction system that can persist without direct principal participation, reshape the alternatives reaching principals, and separate participation from accountability. The model identifies activity conditions, capability–structure alignment, and authorization as antecedents; bilateral representation and interaction displacement as mechanisms; and symbolic concentration and representative-centered organizing as organizational consequences. The framework contributes by challenging the actor-bound conception of participation, identifying bilateral representation as a discontinuity in organizing, and explaining why declining principal participation may coexist with persistent principal accountability and increasingly consequential symbolic appearances. The article concludes with managerial implications and an empirical research agenda focused on recruitment, procurement, customer service, and AI-mediated negotiation.

documents.abstract: Introduction: Burnout among nurses is an important occupational health concern because persistent physical and emotional exhaustion may compromise work performance, quality of care, and patient safety. Workload, work-related stress, and shift work are frequently considered important occupational determinants of burnout, particularly among nurses working in high-intensity clinical units. This study aimed to examine the associations of workload, work stress, and shift work with burnout among nurses at Jaury Jusuf Putera Academic Hospital, Makassar, Indonesia. Research Methodology: A quantitative cross-sectional study was conducted among 36 nurses working in the Intensive Care Unit and Emergency Department. Total sampling was applied. Data were collected using structured questionnaires and analyzed using the Chi-square test. Crude odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were derived from the reported 2×2 contingency tables to describe the magnitude of associations. Results: Of the 36 nurses, 19 (52.8%) experienced high burnout. High workload was not significantly associated with burnout (OR = 2.45; 95% CI: 0.64–9.37; p = 0.187). Nurses with moderate work stress had substantially higher odds of high burnout than those with mild stress (OR = 9.00; 95% CI: 1.97–41.08; p = 0.003). Shift work was also significantly associated with burnout (p = 0.047); nurses classified in the high-shift category had lower crude odds of high burnout than those in the low-shift category (OR = 0.25; 95% CI: 0.06–1.01). Conclusion: Work stress and shift work were significantly associated with burnout, whereas workload was not. Hospital management should prioritize stress-management strategies, adequate recovery periods, and evidence-based shift scheduling to reduce occupational burnout and support nurses’ well-being and service quality.

This study aims to reveal the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies on shaping news-sharing behavior among university students on social media platforms. It focuses on the level of trust in news content presented through algorithms. The study employed a survey methodology, using a questionnaire to collect data from a random sample of 200 university students. The results showed that AI technologies have become an influential element in organizing the digital news environment through recommendation systems and content ranking based on audience engagement indicators. The results indicated that news-sharing decisions are increasingly influenced by the news's reach and associated engagement levels, with the majority of respondents exhibiting caution before sharing news. The study also revealed a relative awareness of the risks associated with algorithms, such as reduced media diversity and the potential for misinformation.

documents.abstract: Perkembangan e-commerce yang pesat mendorong integrasi Artificial Intelligence (AI) untuk meningkatkan pengalaman belanja konsumen. Namun, mekanisme psikologis internal yang menjembatani interaksi AI dengan keputusan pembelian aktual masih belum konsisten dan sering kali mengabaikan keseimbangan antara jalur kognitif dan afektif. Penelitian kuantitatif eksplanatori ini bertujuan untuk mengembangkan dan menguji model dual-path consumer engagement berbasis AI dalam mendorong keputusan pembelian konsumen e-commerce di Indonesia. Data dikumpulkan melalui kuesioner dari 196 responden pengguna e-commerce , lalu dianalisis menggunakan metode Structural Equation Modeling-Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS). Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa AI berpengaruh langsung yang positif dan signifikan terhadap keputusan pembelian konsumen. Selain itu, AI terbukti memiliki kontribusi yang sangat besar dalam membentuk Cognitive Engagement dan Affective Engagement. Model struktural membuktikan bahwa Cognitive Engagement berperan secara positif sebagai variabel pemoderasi yang memperkuat pengaruh AI terhadap keputusan pembelian. Sebaliknya, Affective Engagement tidak bertindak sebagai pemoderasi melainkan menjadi pendorong langsung (direct driver) yang masif bagi keputusan pembelian. Kesimpulannya, penyedia platform e-commerce harus menyeimbangkan efisiensi fitur kognitif berbasis AI dengan pendekatan emosional guna mengunci loyalitas dan keputusan transaksi konsumen digital secara berkelanjutan.

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence, also known as AI, is transforming the modern workplace by making employees more efficient at analyzing, creating, admin and decision making. Modern AI systems have the capability of handling vast amounts of data, identifying patterns, creating content, summarizing information, offering recommendations, and conversing in natural language. These capabilities are driving organizations to adopt a model where technology and employees work together rather than the traditional automation model. But, human-AI collaboration doesn't just happen by simply introducing an AI tool. It relies on employee capability, trust, transparency, organizational preparedness, governance of data, security of privacy, and defined humans' role. This paper explores the concept of human–AI collaboration and its impact on productivity, decision-making, creativity, learning, customer service, and organizational performance. It creates a conceptual framework that unfolds around five related dimensions: AI capability, human capability, interaction and trust, organizational readiness, and responsible AI governance. The paper also evaluates the challenges that include job transformation, algorithmic bias, lack of explainability, privacy and security concerns, skill deficits, change resistance, and overreliance on AI. A human-in-the-loop approach is suggested, to enable the level of human involvement to correspond to the risk of the task. The paper argues that the best model for the workplace is not one that pits man against machine, but one that uses AI to drive computational power and leaves judgment, creativity, context, ethics, interpersonal responsibility, and accountability to the humans. The activity encompassed discussions on AI's role in decision-making, its impact on productivity, the future of work, responsible AI, and the skills required to work alongside AI.

documents.abstract: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into academic workflows has significantly transformed the landscape of scholarly writing. This paper explores the application of AI tools in structuring academic papers, with a specific focus on how generative AI and large language models (LLMs) can assist researchers in organizing complex data and adhering to rigorous publishing standards. By analyzing the traditional challenges associated with academic structuring—such as maintaining logical flow, formatting citations, and organizing the IMRaD (Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion) framework—this paper demonstrates how AI can be utilized as an assistive technology to enhance efficiency and coherence. Furthermore, the paper critically examines the limitations and ethical considerations of AI-assisted writing, including the risks of fabricated citations (hallucinations) and the importance of preserving human critical thinking. Ultimately, this paper argues that while AI offers powerful structural scaffolding for academic manuscripts, it must be deployed as a supportive tool rather than a replacement for human intellectual rigor and academic integrity.

Artificial Intelligence has really transformed areas like healthcare, legal services, education, finance, and business. But its quick spread also brings persistent tech troubles, mainly the confusing issue of AI mistakes, errors, and misinformation. Large Language Models (LLMs) can handle all sorts of tasks, from text creation and code writing to answering questions and summarizing info. Still, despite their big achievements, LLMs sometimes spout incorrect stuff – factually wrong or made-up content – which is called "hallucination." This paper dives deep into AI failures, showing how they differ based on errors in logic, generated fiction presented confidently, and correct data being misinterpreted. It looks at why AI systems act overly sure of themselves, how messy training data messes up, and ideas for fixing this like boosted retrieval methods, cleaner training data, and humans checking the work. What stands out is that these glitches aren't just random tech snafus. Instead, they're a design quirk of big AI language models. Fixing them demands teamwork from folks in various fields, not just developers. So, while there are big issues, figuring out ways to collaborate could make these systems way more reliable in the future.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly used by university students to compare alternatives, obtain recommendations, and support academic decisions. This study examines whether objective AI literacy and perceived reliability can predict student trust in generative AI-assisted decision-making. A cross-sectional online survey yielded 406 responses. After eligibility screening, 310 respondents met the inclusion criteria, and 280 respondents who passed the attention check served as the primary analysis sample. AI literacy was measured using 12 multiple-choice questions, while perceived reliability and user trust were measured on a five-point scale. Item analysis supported the removal of two negatively worded items that had low item-total correlations. Multiple linear regression with HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors showed that the model explained 52.1% of the variance in user trust. Perceived reliability was the dominant predictor (standardized beta = 0.704; p < 0.001), whereas AI literacy provided a smaller positive contribution (standardized beta = 0.101; p = 0.022). The AI literacy coefficient was non-significant in a sensitivity analysis that retained all eligible respondents. These findings indicate that student trust primarily depends on the assessment that generative AI outputs are accurate, consistent, relevant, and reliable. Higher education institutions need to integrate AI literacy education with verification practices so that students are capable of assessing system reliability before using AI recommendations.

documents.abstract: The chapter looks on how AI systems and other advanced IT solutions can be used in connection to human modelling activities. AI has been used in this sense more than 30 years, earlier with focus on the use of symbolic AI. Various approaches have lately been using existing data for doing modelling on a higher abstraction level, with a focus in recent years on the use of a generative AI. More traditional machine learning also plays a greater role in support of human modelling. In model-driven engineering, the focus was later on generating code from models. Now, code can, to a larger extent, be generated from existing code using generative AI. On the other hand, other usages of models for analysis and design are still areas where the human must be clearly in the loop, due to that e.g. analysis and requirements models must still be developed through social construction. In our neuro-conceptualisation research, we analyse biometric data to eventually develop neuro-adaptive modelling systems for areas where human modelling is important.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence has become a dominant technology in digital business and has greatly changed how businesses interact with customers. Digital businesses increasingly use AI-based technologies to deliver convenient, personalized services. Such technologies include Chatbots, virtual assistants, recommendation systems, personalized advertisements, automated customer support, and AI-powered search. These developments have changed customer expectations and affected their willingness to use and continue using digital services. Therefore, businesses operating in a thriving digital environment must understand AI from the customer’s perspective. The study covers a broad spectrum of AI dimensions, including personalization, efficiency, ease of use, responsiveness, reliability, service quality, security, and privacy. These factors are expected to influence customers’ behavioral intentions, including buying behavior, usage, purchasing patterns, and recommending AI-enabled digital services. The study also investigates “Customer experience and Customer engagement as mediators” to understand how AI impacts customers’ behavioral responses. The study has adopted a quantitative research approach. The study collects primary data through a questionnaire from customers with experience using AI-enabled digital business services. The study measures customers’ perceptions and behavioral intentions using a five-point Likert scale. The study uses descriptive statistics, correlation, and regression to examine the relationships among AI, Customer experience, Customer engagement, and behavioral intention. The findings provide a clearer view of AI’s effect on consumer behavior, helping digital businesses enhance convenience, personalization, Customer engagement & experience; address privacy & security concerns; build customer trust; and encourage continued use of AI-enabled digital services.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in diagnosis, clinical decision support, patient monitoring, and treatment planning, but its integration complicates the allocation of legal responsibility when patients are harmed. This article examines whether the legal frameworks of Türkiye and the European Union adequately protect patients where clinical decisions are shaped by AI systems. Using comparative doctrinal legal analysis, it evaluates professional negligence, institutional duties, product liability, data protection, informed consent, and evidentiary barriers. It argues that physician-centred liability is insufficient when relevant knowledge, control, and preventive capacity are distributed among clinicians, healthcare institutions, technology providers, and regulators. The article develops the Distributed Accountability Framework for AI-Driven Healthcare (DAF-AIH), which maps responsibility across four dimensions—clinical, institutional, technological, and regulatory—and identifies meaningful human oversight, patient-centred transparency, and effective access to evidence as cross-cutting safeguards. The framework does not create automatic collective liability; it offers a structured method for tracing legally relevant duties, control, omissions, and causal contribution. The comparison highlights both the regulatory resources and unresolved remedial gaps in Türkiye and the EU.

documents.abstract: Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mengkaji implementasi aplikasi SRIKANDI (Sistem Informasi Kearsipan Dinamis Terintegrasi) terhadap produktivitas tenaga administrasi di Madrasah Aliyah Negeri (MAN) Kota Surabaya. Penelitian menggunakan metode kualitatif deskriptif dengan pengumpulan data melalui wawancara mendalam kepada tiga informan yang dipilih secara purposif berdasarkan representasi pengguna: Kepala Tata Usaha, tenaga administrasi senior, dan pegawai baru. Temuan penelitian memperlihatkan berdasarkan persepsi informan bahwa pemanfaatan aplikasi SRIKANDI berkontribusi dalam peningkatan efisiensi waktu kerja, penghematan biaya operasional, kemudahan dalam memantau kinerja berdasarkan data, serta percepatan penelusuran arsip. Namun demikian, implementasinya masih menghadapi sejumlah kendala yang dikategorikan ke dalam faktor manusia (human factor), faktor teknis (technical factor), dan faktor organisasi (organizational factor). Berdasarkan hasil penelitian tersebut, dapat disimpulkan bahwa keberhasilan transformasi administrasi digital tidak semata-mata ditentukan oleh kualitas teknologi, melainkan juga oleh kesiapan sumber daya manusia dan komitmen organisasi.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is now widely used in academic and daily activities, yet its acceptance may differ across user groups. This study measures the level of AI acceptance among university students and the general public, examines the effect of perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness on behavioral intention, and tests differences between the two groups. A quantitative survey based on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) was conducted with 49 respondents (30 students and 19 members of the public). Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, path analysis, and the Mann–Whitney test. AI acceptance was high (M = 3,60). Perceived ease of use significantly affected perceived usefulness (β = 0,830) and behavioral intention (β = 0,448), whereas the effect of perceived usefulness on behavioral intention was not significant (β = 0,280). Behavioral intention positively affected daily AI use (β = 0,411) but explained only a small share of its variance (R² = 0,169). No significant differences were found between students and the public on any variable. The findings suggest that ease of use is the key to AI adoption, so simple interfaces and user training should be prioritised.

AI tools (ChatGPT, Grammarly, Gemini, QuillBot) are increasingly used in higher education to support learning and writing, but concerns exist about learner dependency and its impact on critical thinking and independent learning. This study examined the association between AI reliance and critical thinking among students from five Kenyan universities. Using a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design, data were collected from 275 students via questionnaires. Quantitative analysis included descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, regression, and ANOVA. Results showed moderate AI reliance for tasks such as assignment preparation and idea generation. A modest positive correlation was found between AI use and critical thinking (r=0.24, p < 0.05). Self-directed learning (β = 0.29) and purposeful AI use (β = 0.21) were significantly associated with critical thinking. ANOVA indicated that moderate AI users had higher critical thinking scores than those reporting low or excessive AI use.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping teaching, learning, and research by offering tools that can support educational practice and academic work. This paper examines AI applications in education, their potential benefits, associated challenges, and ethical implications. It considers how AI can assist teachers with lesson planning, instructional materials, assessment, and feedback; support students through personalized learning and explanations of academic concepts; and help researchers with literature searches, data analysis, reference organization, and academic writing. Drawing on a review of existing literature, the paper identifies opportunities to improve educational efficiency, accessibility, and academic productivity. It also highlights concerns involving data privacy, algorithmic bias, inaccurate outputs, academic dishonesty, unequal access to technology, and overdependence on AI tools. The literature points to the importance of user training, ethical guidelines, institutional support, and critical evaluation of AI-generated content (Maphalala & Ajani, 2025; Khatri & Karki, 2023). The paper argues that AI should complement—not replace—teachers, learners, and researchers. Responsible integration requires a balance between technological innovation and human judgment, creativity, critical thinking, and academic integrity.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence can assist audit analysis while changing how professionals evaluate evidence and accept advice. This systematic literature review examines the evidence supporting concerns about over-reliance on AI in audit decision-making. An OpenAlex title-and-abstract search and supplementary Consensus and SciSpace searches conducted on 29 October 2026 identified 149 records. After deduplication and eligibility assessment, 12 empirical journal studies were included. Five experimental reports, five surveys and two qualitative studies were synthesised using a design-sensitive approach and a six-domain critical appraisal. The experimental evidence more clearly demonstrates context-dependent advice-taking and algorithm aversion than the prevalence of inappropriate acceptance of incorrect AI advice. Survey associations between technology use, trust and reported scepticism do not establish behavioural calibration. Qualitative findings identify responsibility and professional learning as consequential organisational concerns. A proposed framework distinguishes output validity, trust, verification, reliance and defensible judgement, and generates four propositions for future testing. Practical implications include access to contradictory evidence, evaluation of both acceptance and rejection errors, and review that examines reasons for reliance. Limited search coverage, inaccessible reports, version differences, partial full-text access and an AI-assisted singleworkflow process constrain confidence. The review supports proportionate safeguards and better behavioural measurement without estimating a population rate of auditor over-reliance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The article examines the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the didactics of Latin, framing AI as a transformative epistemic mediator rather than a mere technological adjunct. In the evolving digital landscape, AI is reshaping educational processes by influencing how knowledge is accessed, structured, and interpreted. The study critically explores four key areas—adaptive learning, gamification, assisted translation, and digital resources—demonstrating how AI can enhance pedagogical personalization, engagement, and inclusive learning experiences. Special attention is given to the challenges posed by algorithmic opacity, teacher mediation, and the ethical tensions surrounding automation in educational settings. The Latin language, understood as a symbolic and logical construct, is presented as uniquely suited to benefit from AI-enhanced learning environments, which can support complex interpretive practices. When implemented within a coherent pedagogical framework, critically and ethically, AI has the potential to revitalize classical language teaching, enhance students’ interpretive skills and metalinguistic skills, foster both critical literacy and meaningful interaction with classical texts. Ultimately, this contribution argues for a humanistic and ethically grounded approach on AI integration in education: Latin and AI together offer new avenues for promoting critical thinking and cultural awareness in education, reaffirming the relevance of classical studies in the digital age. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Inclusion; Teacher Education; Latin Didactics; Inclusive Technologies.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence AI is getting more and more involved in higher education, it is reshaping teaching, learning , assessment, academic administration, research, and even how institutions decide things. In the last few years the fast rise of generative artificial intelligence GenAI, plus intelligent tutoring systems, learning analytics, automated assessment, recommendation systems, and AI assisted administrative tools has opened up new possibilities for universities, yet it also brings worries like academic integrity, data privacy, algorithmic bias, digital inequality, transparency, and changing professional roles. This paper actually uses a secondary-data based systematic review, looking at research and policy sources about AI and digital transformation in higher education. The review brings together outcomes from academic studies, other systematic reviews, and international policy frameworks, sort of to map out the main uses, opportunities, obstacles, and the kind of emerging trends that are starting to show up. What the literature suggests is that AI in education is not only about making content. It also includes adaptive learning, personalized tutoring, intelligent assessment, profiling and prediction, and support for institutional management. At the same time, good adoption does not just happen, it needs institutional policies, AI literacy, ethical safety nets, teacher professional development, careful responsible assessment approaches, and a human centered way of putting things into practice. A number of recent international frameworks stress human agency, ethics, AI competencies, and responsible usage, so there is a clear direction there. Overall the review shows that AI is best understood as augmentation tech with AI to help educators and learners not to flip a switch and replace the educational roles that already exist. For digital transformation a balance must exist, with technical novelty on one side and pedagogical sense together with ethical norms institutional realities and human factors, on the other. None of those should be treated as optional because leaving one out tends to break the system quickly.

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is one of the most significant technological developments of the 21st century, and it is impacting the global job market in profound ways. AI-powered tools like machine learning, robotics, natural language processing, and automation have transformed the nature of work, the productivity of industries and countries, and the skills that the workforce needs in developed and developing countries. This research paper analyses change in employment, job displacement, skill transformation, productivity increases, wage inequality, and labour market polarization caused by the impact of AI on the global labour market. The study also explores changes in manufacturing, healthcare, financial services, retail, logistics, education and information technology by sector. This study is qualitative and quantitative, based on secondary data obtained from international organizations like the International Labour Organization (ILO), the World Economic Forum (WEF), the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the International Monetary Fund (IMF), and the World Bank (WB). The analysis of the data from 2018 to 2025 will provide insights into the evolving employment landscape as a result of AI adoption. The study highlights the potential of AI to boost productivity, efficiency, and economic growth, as well as the challenges it poses, such as job displacement, technological unemployment, growing income inequality, and skill mismatches. The results indicate that repetitive and routine occupations are most likely to be automated, while creative, emotionally intelligent, and advanced analytical jobs grow. The paper also delves into the new roles in data science, AI engineering, cybersecurity, digital marketing, and human-machine collaboration. The developing countries have different challenges because of poor digital infrastructure, low technological readiness and inadequate training of the workforce. Developed economies, on the other hand, have the better option to adapt via innovation ecosystems and skill development programs. The study emphasizes the importance of governments, educational institutions, multinational corporations, and international organizations to make working life easier for people with disabilities to transition into and out of. The paper argues that AI does not only pose a threat, and is not an automatic assurance of economic well-being, but rather the impact of AI relies on policy response, workforce adaptability and technological ethical governance. Therefore, public policies to promote reskilling and lifelong learning, labour protection, digital inclusion and social security systems are required to ensure the sustainability of employment in the face of technology. The study suggests a collective global governance approach to ensure equitable distribution of the opportunities of AI-enabled economic transformation across societies and labour markets globally. The objectives, as well as the concepts of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Lay of the Land – Labour Market, Employment Trends, Job Displacement, AI's contribution to GDP growth, Workforce Transformation and Digital Skills and Policy recommendations, will be addressed.

documents.abstract: This report presents a literature review and discussion focused on the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to support future flight operations, particularly within the context of Single Pilot Operations (SPO) and failure mitigation. The scope considered focuses on flight deck operations that support decision-making, reduce pilot workload, and improve situational awareness, with a special emphasis on processes for detecting and reducing the effects of system or aircraft-level failures. Although failure management is a widely studied topic in the aeronautical context (Zolghadri, 2024), there are still few systematic reviews on the specific combination of SPO and AI, even though several isolated studies and reports highlighting the importance of the subject have been published, as discussed in this text.

Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in schools creates opportunities for instructional innovation but also raises questions concerning governance, professional judgement, and institutional readiness. This study examined AI integration and governance in selected United Arab Emirates (UAE) schools and developed a leadership-guided implementation framework. An exploratory sequential mixed-methods design combined semi-structured interviews with 10 purposively selected teachers and school leaders and a subsequent structured survey of 80 respondents, selected through stratified sampling. Interview transcripts underwent thematic analysis; quantitative responses were analysed using weighted means, standard deviations, and Pearson product–moment correlations at the .05 significance level. Seven qualitative themes clustered into AI integration and AI governance. Overall AI integration was rated moderate (grand weighted mean [GWM] = 3.41), with adaptive integration highest (3.76), followed by professional productivity (3.38) and AI-enhanced teaching (3.08). Overall AI governance was high (GWM = 3.32), led by ethical governance (3.66), followed by strategic governance (3.34), organisational support (3.34), and uneven governance (2.97). Organisational support was significantly associated with all three AI-integration dimensions, while adaptive integration had its strongest observed association with ethical governance (r = .539, p < .001). Integrated findings informed the proposed Leadership-Guided AI Integration and Governance Framework for UAE Schools, emphasising pedagogical use, human oversight, ethical safeguards, strategic leadership, professional learning, and institutional readiness. The proposed framework is a study-derived practical output, not a causally validated model.

documents.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) within telemedicine has revolutionized virtual healthcare delivery by enabling high-precision diagnostics and tailored treatment strategies remotely. This paper evaluates state-of-the-art AI models applied to medical imaging and clinical text data within telehealth platforms, highlighting significant improvements in diagnostic accuracy and clinical decision support. Using deep learning architectures like ResNet-50 for imaging and BERT for natural language processing of electronic health records, the framework demonstrates enhanced patient care personalization and operational efficiency. Survey feedback from clinicians and patients underscores AI's practical benefits in improving healthcare accessibility and quality in remote settings. Challenges, including algorithmic biases and data privacy risks, are discussed, along with future research directions aimed at sustaining AI-driven telemedicine enhancements to health systems worldwide.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Introduction: Feedback is central to medical education, and generative artificial intelligence (AI) has made individualized, timely, and scalable feedback possible. Questions remain, however, about its accuracy, contextual relevance, and capacity to promote learning compared with feedback from faculty and clinical supervisors. Objective: To analyze the evidence on AI-generated feedback compared with human feedback in medical education, considering its quality, educational effectiveness, applicability, and limitations. Methods: Integrative review structured with the PICo strategy. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and LILACS were searched for studies published between January 2020 and October 2026 in English, Portuguese, or Spanish. Studies were classified by level of evidence, and findings were synthesized through interpretive thematic analysis. Results: Eleven studies from Canada, the United States, Germany, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Japan were included: five randomized trials (level II) and six comparative descriptive or mixed-methods studies (level VI). AI-generated feedback generally matched or exceeded human feedback in comprehensiveness, consistency, and adherence to predefined criteria, especially in written, structured, and simulated tasks. Human feedback was superior in clarity, relevance, and accuracy in some studies and in more complex diagnostic and therapeutic situations. Learning outcomes were measured only in the short term, and hybrid models combining AI data with faculty input showed favorable results. Conclusion: AI can increase the availability and consistency of feedback but does not replace the clinical and pedagogical judgment of faculty. Supervised integration of both modalities is the most consistent approach, and studies with longer-term outcomes and Latin American settings are needed.

documents.abstract: This study examines the extent to which generative artificial intelligence tools (ChatGPT, Gemini, and DeepSeek) can generate middle school geometry questions aligned with the cognitive levels of Bloom’s Revised Taxonomy. The study also evaluates the quality and taxonomic appropriateness of these questions based on expert judgments. A convergent parallel mixed-methods design was employed. A total of 30 geometry questions, including open-ended and multiple-choice items, were generated by the AI tools using structured prompts. Ten mathematics education experts evaluated each question using a rubric that assessed alignment with the intended Bloom level. Quantitative data were analyzed using frequencies, percentages, and Gwet’s AC1 agreement coefficient, while qualitative data were analyzed through thematic content analysis to identify patterns in expert justifications. The findings indicate that all three AI tools perform relatively well at lower and middle cognitive levels (understanding, applying, and analyzing), whereas their performance declines at higher levels (evaluating and creating). DeepSeek and Gemini showed higher overall alignment with targeted cognitive levels compared to ChatGPT. However, expert agreement decreased significantly at higher-order levels, indicating inconsistencies in how these levels are interpreted and represented. Qualitative findings revealed issues related to insufficient cognitive depth, weak distractors in multiple-choice items, and mismatches between intended and actual cognitive levels. Overall, the results highlight both the potential and limitations of generative AI in educational assessment and emphasize the necessity of expert supervision in ensuring pedagogical and taxonomic accuracy.This study compares the performance of three generative artificial intelligence tools—ChatGPT, Gemini, and DeepSeek—in generating questions aligned with Bloom’s six cognitive levels in middle school geometry. The participants consisted of ten mathematics teachers with expertise in mathematics education. The teachers evaluated the AI-generated questions for alignment with the intended cognitive level and provided judgments on their taxonomic appropriateness and overall quality. Quantitative analyses examined the agreement between the intended cognitive level and the levels assigned by participants. In addition, qualitative content analysis was used to analyze participants’ evaluations and comments. The findings highlight both the potential and limitations of generative AI tools and emphasize the importance of expert supervision in AI-supported assessment practices.

Student engagement positively influences academic achievement, yet instruments suited to the Indonesian cultural context remain limited. This study aimed to develop a valid, reliable, and user-friendly student engagement scale for high school students. Using a quantitative descriptive design, the study involved 295 male and female students aged 15–18 years recruited through convenience sampling. The scale comprised three dimensions: behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement. The results showed that the scale demonstrated a good model fit based on the goodness-of-fit indices (χ2/df = 1.60; CFI = 0.966; TLI = 0.962; SRMR = 0.074; RMSEA = 0.045) and good reliability, with Cronbach’s alpha values of 0.844 for emotional engagement, 0.753 for behavioral engagement, and 0.782 for cognitive engagement. The developed scale can be used by teachers, counselors, and educational researchers to identify students’ levels of engagement and inform the development of programs to improve student engagement.

AI-supported English speaking offers opportunities for rehearsal and feedback, yet the relationship between perceived AI usefulness and learners’ self-perceived communicative competence remains insufficiently understood. This cross-sectional study examined associations among perceived usefulness, intrinsic motivation, higher-order engagement, deep and surface learning, and self-perceived communicative competence. Survey data from 420 Vietnamese undergraduate and postgraduate students with experience in AI-supported English speaking were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling. Engagement was conceptualised as a reflective higher-order construct comprising behavioural, cognitive, and agentic dimensions. The findings revealed positive associations between perceived usefulness and intrinsic motivation, as well as between intrinsic motivation and engagement. Engagement was positively associated with deep learning and self-perceived communicative competence (β = .460), but negatively associated with surface learning. Deep and surface learning also showed significant associations with communicative self-perceptions in opposite directions, although their direct associations were weaker than that of engagement. The model explained 35.0% of the variance in self-perceived communicative competence, rather than objectively assessed speaking proficiency. These findings highlight the importance of purposeful interaction, critical evaluation of AI feedback, and learner-initiated clarification in fostering meaningful English-speaking practice beyond AI use alone. Longitudinal studies incorporating direct speaking assessments are needed to determine whether these associations extend to actual communicative performance.

The rapid adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the accounting profession, creating opportunities for enhanced efficiency while raising concerns regarding employees’ adaptability, job security, and long-term engagement. This conceptual study proposes an integrated framework for examining Sustainable Employee Engagement (SEE) among accounting professionals in Malaysia. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory (SDT), the framework investigates AI adoption, perceived organizational support, and job security as key technological and organizational factors influencing SEE through the mediating role of technology self-efficacy. SEE extends conventional employee engagement by emphasizing employees’ capacity to sustain physical, cognitive, emotional, and behavioural involvement while maintaining adaptability, well-being, and professional relevance during continuous technological transformation. The proposed framework suggests that supportive organizational conditions, employment stability, and effective AI adoption strengthen employees’ confidence in learning, using, and adapting to emerging technologies, thereby fostering sustainable engagement. The study contributes to the literature by positioning technology self-efficacy as a psychological mechanism linking technological and organizational conditions with SEE. Practically, the framework provides guidance for accounting firms and HRD practitioners in developing training, digital upskilling, organizational support, and talent management strategies that promote a resilient, adaptable, and sustainably engaged accounting workforce in AI-enabled workplaces.

Road agencies are investing in artificial intelligence to inspect pavements, forecast deterioration and plan maintenance, yet the value of these tools ultimately depends on whether they improve the interventions that are funded and delivered. This critical narrative review examines the gap between predictive performance and intervention quality in pavement maintenance, termed here the artificial intelligence intervention gap. Literature was identified through structured searches of multidisciplinary and regional scholarly indexes, supplemented by citation tracking and institutional sources, and was appraised for design adequacy, validation practice, causal identification and decision relevance. The synthesis is organised along a decision chain that runs from sensing and condition assessment, through deterioration prediction and estimation of treatment effects, to optimisation, implementation and outcome feedback. The evidence is strongest for automated distress detection and short-term condition prediction, where deep learning and ensemble models frequently achieve high accuracy on benchmark or single-agency data. Confidence weakens progressively along the chain. Performance claims rarely survive transfer across regions, survey technologies or time periods, validation designs often ignore spatial and temporal dependence, and explanations derived from post hoc attribution methods are commonly interpreted as causal mechanisms. Treatment effects are usually inferred from observational records in which maintenance was assigned according to condition, so selection bias and endogeneity remain largely unaddressed outside a small econometric and causal-inference literature. Reinforcement learning and metaheuristic planning studies report cost savings, but most are trained and evaluated within simulators built from the same associational models, and few compare recommended policies with realised outcomes. Implementation evidence, including digital twins and language-model assistants, is at an early, largely demonstrative stage. The review argues that pavement maintenance requires an evidence-based decision-making standard in which intervention effects are explicitly identified, uncertainty is propagated into decisions, decision quality rather than prediction error is the primary evaluation criterion, and agencies monitor the outcomes of recommended treatments. Priorities include benchmark datasets with recorded interventions, quasi-experimental and pragmatic field evaluations of treatments, decision-focused model training and prospective comparison of algorithmic and conventional programmes.

Remote and hybrid work arrangements are now enduring features of work design, yet evidence on their relationship with employee behavioral health remains mixed. Guided by the Job Demands–Resources framework, this study examined whether work modality (onsite, hybrid, or remote) is associated with perceived stress and social isolation, and whether perceived organizational support and gender moderate these associations. Secondary cross-sectional survey data from 2,544 employees were analyzed using correlation analysis, multiple linear regression for social isolation, ordinal logistic regression for stress, and interaction-based moderation models, supplemented by regression diagnostics, confidence intervals, effect sizes, and statistical power analysis. Hybrid and remote employees did not differ significantly from onsite employees in social isolation or stress, and neither organizational support nor gender moderated these relationships. The models explained only 0.1 to 0.2 percent of outcome variance, far below the conventional threshold for a small effect, even though the design had high power to detect small effects. Because the source dataset is synthetic, the findings describe this dataset and require replication with real workforce data. The results suggest that broad work-location categories have limited value as standalone indicators of employee behavioral health, and that well-being strategies should focus on the demands and resources surrounding work, including workload, social connection, work–life boundaries, managerial accessibility, and individualized support.

Numerous primary school students reveal low learning motivation in social studies because the material is abstract and less relevant to their lives. An innovative learning model that integrates local cultural values is needed to make learning more interesting and meaningful. This study aims to test the effectiveness of a social studies learning model that contains character values of the local wisdom tradition in increasing the learning motivation of elementary students. Local wisdom from Sumatra has values of togetherness, unity, and collective spirit that can be integrated into character education. The study used a quasi-experimental design with a post-test-only control group design model involving three fourth-grade classes, consisting of two experimental classes and one control class. Data were collected through a learning motivation questionnaire based on cognitive motivation theory and analyzed using one-way ANOVA and the LSD post hoc test. The results reveal a significant difference in learning motivation between groups, with the highest score shown by the class that received learning based on local wisdom character values. This finding indicates that the integration of local cultural values in social studies learning is effective in building students' intrinsic motivation. This model is an innovative alternative in developing character education that is contextual and relevant to students' cultural backgrounds.

This paper argues that the central problem posed by contemporary artificial intelligence is not whether computational systems can reproduce the observable functions of human cognition, but whether their expanding integration into social institutions encourages a reduction of human judgment, creativity, and collective autonomy to measurable and optimizable processes. I address Geoffrey Hinton’s assertion that AI models can obtain consciousness as a starting point for a further investigation of digital barbarism, the trend to imaginatively personify digital applications. Drawing on Thomas Nagel's account of subjective experience and Cornelius Castoriadis' theory of the social imaginary, I develop a critique of algorithmic reductionism that distinguishes the phenomenological limits of computational explanations from the political consequences of deploying AI within corporate and technocratic institutions. I argue that the democratic challenge of AI lies in preserving the capacity of individuals and communities to create new social significations, deliberate about collective ends, and determine the institutional conditions of their technological lives
